title: Earthquake Preparedness in Istanbul: Before, During and After
excerpt: Istanbul sits near an active fault. What to check before you rent, how compulsory earthquake insurance (DASK) works, your assembly area, an emergency bag, and what to do during and after a quake.
bodyHtml:
Istanbul lies close to the North Anatolian Fault, which runs beneath the Marmara Sea. The 1999 İzmit earthquake devastated the region, and on 23 April 2025 a magnitude 6.2 earthquake off Silivri shook the whole city. Nobody can predict when the next large earthquake will come, and you should ignore anyone who claims to. What you can do is prepare — and most of it takes an afternoon.

This guide is practical information drawn from official Turkish sources, not professional or engineering advice.

Before: where you live matters most

The building you live in is the biggest factor in how an earthquake affects you. Before you rent, ask:

  • When was the building constructed? Building codes have been tightened over the years, most recently in 2018. A newer building is not automatically safe and an older one is not automatically unsafe, but the question is worth asking.

  • Has it been assessed or strengthened? Ask whether the building has had a structural assessment or retrofitting. A formal risk assessment of a building is applied for by its owners through the Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change or the municipality — as a tenant, ask your landlord.

  • Does it have compulsory earthquake insurance (DASK)? See below.

AFAD's Türkiye Earthquake Hazard Map (you log in with e-Devlet) shows how strongly the ground may shake at a location. It describes the ground, not the building — it cannot tell you whether a particular building is safe.

Compulsory earthquake insurance (DASK)

Compulsory Earthquake Insurance, issued through the Natural Disaster Insurance Institution (DASK), is required for residential buildings under Law No. 6305. It is checked when property is bought or sold and when electricity or water subscriptions are opened or transferred.

  • It is normally taken out by the owner, but a tenant can also take out the policy.

  • It covers damage to the building up to a set limit. It does not cover your furniture, electronics or other belongings — that needs separate home contents insurance (konut sigortası).

  • You can check whether an address has a policy on DASK's website, or call Alo DASK on 125.

Know your assembly area

Assembly areas (toplanma alanları) are open spaces chosen as safe places to gather in the first hours after a disaster. Find yours before you need it:

  • e-Devlet: search for "Acil Toplanma Alanı Sorgulama" after logging in. Foreigners with a residence permit can get e-Devlet access.

  • AFAD Acil app: shows assembly areas on a map and lets you call or message 112 with your location. Registration asks for your phone number and an identity number.

  • Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality city map (sehirharitasi.ibb.gov.tr) also shows assembly and temporary shelter areas.

Agree on a meeting point with the people you live with — and with friends — in case phones don't work.

Prepare an emergency bag

AFAD recommends keeping a disaster and emergency bag somewhere easy to grab. Its list includes:

  • Drinking water and long-lasting, high-energy food for everyone in the household

  • A first-aid kit, and any medicines you take regularly with their prescriptions

  • A torch, a battery-powered radio and spare batteries

  • A whistle, a pocket knife, scissors, tape and a plastic sheet

  • A blanket or sleeping bag, and clothes suitable for the season

  • A hygiene kit, some cash, paper and a pen

  • Copies of important documents — for you, that means your passport and residence permit

  • Food and water for pets for three days, and anything specific to children, older people or people with disabilities in your household

Check expiry dates and refresh the bag every six months.

During an earthquake

If you are indoors, Drop, Cover, Hold On (Çök-Kapan-Tutun): get down, protect your head and neck, and hold on next to or under a sturdy piece of furniture until the shaking stops. Stay where you are while it shakes.

  • Keep away from windows, balconies, bookcases, kitchen cupboards and anything that can fall.

  • Don't run for the door, the stairs or the lift.

  • Outdoors: move away from buildings, power lines, trees and poles to open ground.

  • In a vehicle: pull over away from buildings and overhead hazards and stay inside.

After the shaking stops

  • Turn off gas, electricity and water.

  • Leave by the stairs, never the lift, and go to your assembly area. Stay out of damaged buildings — aftershocks follow.

  • Call 112 for emergencies. Keep other calls short so the network stays free; the AFAD Acil app can send messages when calls don't get through.

  • If you are trapped, don't light matches or lighters, cover your mouth and nose, and tap on pipes or use a whistle rather than shouting.

Staying informed

AFAD and the Kandilli Observatory publish every recorded earthquake, usually within minutes. Rely on them and ignore rumours and "predictions" circulating on social media.

If you are a foreign national, check whether your country's embassy or consulate offers registration for its citizens in Türkiye, so they can reach you in an emergency.
